text:
In Genesis 22 the God who promises and the God who demands are set down side by side, and the narrator makes no choice between them; neither is reconciled to the other. The reader is placed where Abraham stood upon the mountain, with the knife raised and the ram not yet seen. The question the story raises cannot be answered, and its being unanswerable is the only answer the narrator affords. Whoever reads the chapter with attention is put to a trial of his own.

Genesis 22 is, in this light, more a story about reading than a story about sacrifice, and its lesson is that the most important things are those a text leaves unsaid. Abraham keeps silence; Isaac asks his question; Sarah is absent; the narrator will neither explain nor comment. Each of these is a gap, and each lays its demand upon the reader. The spare economy of the style is the reader's burden, and what the narrator withholds is what the reader is given.
